title: From a $3,000 Tax Refund to 150 Farms: The Diaspora Spice Co. Cookbook Is a Love Letter to Indian Agriculture
excerpt: Oakland-based Sana Javeri Kadri new cookbook pairs 85 recipes with the stories of the regenerative farmers who grow the spices — and it might just change how the diaspora thinks about its pantry.
body:
Most Indian-American kitchens have a spice drawer that tells a familiar story: half-empty jars of ground turmeric bought at the nearest grocery chain, a bag of cumin seeds from Patel Brothers, maybe a tin of garam masala that has been there since the last Diwali. Sana Javeri Kadri wants to blow that drawer wide open.

Her new book, *The Diaspora Spice Co. Cookbook: Seasonal Home Cooking from South Asia's Best Spice Farms*, published by Harvest (an imprint of HarperCollins), arrives at a moment when Indian flavors are everywhere in American food culture — turmeric lattes at every cafe, chaat-spiced everything on restaurant menus, cardamom in craft cocktails — yet the people who actually grow those spices remain invisible.

## A $3,000 Bet on a Turmeric Farmer

The book's origin story has the improbable arc of a startup fairy tale, except it involves dirt. In 2017, Kadri was 23 years old, fresh out of Pomona College, when a visit to a turmeric farm on India's western coast changed everything. She used her $3,000 tax refund to buy the entire harvest, arranged export logistics she had never dealt with before, picked up 350 kilograms of turmeric in a borrowed 1970s stick-shift truck at San Francisco International Airport, and stored it all in the basement of her Oakland co-op.

It sold out in four days. Two weeks later, Julia Turshen featured Diaspora Co. in the *New York Magazine* gift guide, and Kadri woke up to 700 orders. Nine years later, Diaspora Spice Co. works with more than 150 regenerative farm partners across India and Sri Lanka, paying 3.9 times above the commodity price for every crop — a direct challenge to the extractive economics that have defined the global spice trade for centuries.

## 85 Recipes, 10 States, 14 Languages

The cookbook itself is the product of three months of travel across 10 Indian states and Sri Lanka, conducted in 14 languages. Co-authored with recipe editor Asha Loupy, it pairs farmer profiles and evocative photography with 85 recipes designed for what Kadri and Loupy call "a global pantry" — dishes adapted for kitchens in Brooklyn and Bangalore alike.

The recipes range from pantry building blocks — a foundational tadka, spice-forward chutneys — to dinner-party centerpieces. There is a pumpkin chutney that materialized in a Kashmir kitchen at the last possible moment before cameras packed up, and strawberry cardamom bars that Kadri describes as "community rituals," the kind of dish that becomes the thing you always bring.

The book highlights farmers from indigenous communities, young changemakers, and multi-generational farming families who are pioneering sustainable and climate-change-resistant agriculture. Each spice profile reads like a short documentary, connecting the powder in your jar to a person, a place, and a practice.

## Why the Diaspora Should Care

For NRIs who grew up watching their parents haggle over spice prices at Indian grocery stores, the Diaspora Co. model inverts a deeply ingrained assumption: that Indian spices should be cheap. Kadri's company has made the case that paying more — and paying it directly to farmers — produces spices that are not just ethically sourced but dramatically more flavorful.

The cookbook extends that argument into the kitchen. "Eating with the people who grow our spices unveils a whole new dimension in our cooking," Kadri and Loupy write. It is a sentiment that resonates with a generation of Indian Americans who are reconnecting with their food heritage, but want to do so on terms that reflect their values around sustainability and fair trade.

A virtual author talk is scheduled for June 23 at 2:00 PM ET, presented by the Ocean County Library, where readers can hear Kadri and Loupy discuss the cookbook and enter to win a copy.

## What's Next

Diaspora Co. continues to expand its regenerative farm network. The company's model — single-origin, farmer-named spices sold at premium prices with full supply-chain transparency — has attracted attention from food industry analysts who see it as a template for how specialty food brands can scale without sacrificing ethics. For the diaspora, the cookbook is an invitation: your grandmother's recipes deserve better spices, and the people who grow them deserve better pay.
